The model in the first tutorial maps covariates to parameters deterministically, so two
patients with the same weight get the same curve. Real patients differ for reasons the
covariates do not capture. The standard pharmacometric answer is a *mixed-effects model*:
every individual `i` gets random effects `ηᵢ`, and their parameters are

```math
z_i = \zeta(x_i) \cdot \exp(\eta_i), \qquad \eta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Omega),
```

where `ζ(x)` is the output of the neural network (the *typical* parameters) and `Ω` the
covariance of the random effects. Together with a residual error model this defines a
likelihood. Here the random effects are inferred with variational inference: each
individual gets a Gaussian posterior `q(ηᵢ) = N(μᵢ, Lᵢ Lᵢᵀ)`, and the network weights,
the posteriors and the error parameters are trained jointly by maximising the evidence
lower bound (ELBO).

```{julia}
using DeepCompartmentModels
using DataFrames, CSV
using CairoMakie
using Random
using Statistics: mean
```

## Data

We use the warfarin concentrations, loaded as in the [data tutorial](05-loading-data.md).

```{julia}
warfarin = DataFrame(CSV.File(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "data", "warfarin.csv")))
warfarin = warfarin[warfarin.DVID .== 1, :]

function make_individual(g)
    covariates = Float32[g.WEIGHT[1], g.AGE[1], g.SEX[1]]
    doses = Matrix{Float32}(g[g.MDV .== 1, [:TIME, :DOSE, :RATE, :DURATION]])
    obs = g[g.MDV .== 0, :]
    return Individual(g.ID[1], covariates, obs.TIME, obs.DV, generate_dosing_callback(doses))
end

population = Population([make_individual(g) for g in groupby(warfarin, :ID)])
length(population)
```

## Model

A one-compartment model with first-order absorption, parameters `[kₐ, CL, V]`, and a
network from weight, age and sex. The final layer scales the outputs to plausible
magnitudes for warfarin (clearance around 0.1 L/h, volume around 10 L).

```{julia}
ann = Lux.Chain(
    Normalize(Float32[100, 100, 1]),
    Lux.Dense(3, 16, tanh),
    Lux.Dense(16, 3, Lux.softplus),
    Lux.WrappedFunction(x -> x .* Float32[1, 0.2, 10]),
)

problem = ODEProblem(one_comp_abs!, zeros(Float32, 2), (-0.1f0, 1f0); dt = 0.01f0)
model = DCM(problem, ann, ProportionalError(0.2f0); target = 2)
```

The third argument is the residual error model. `ProportionalError(0.2f0)` says that
the standard deviation of the observation noise is proportional to the prediction, and
`0.2` is the starting value of that proportion. `AdditiveError` and `CombinedError`
(additive plus proportional) work the same way.

## Step 1: warm-start the typical parameters

Mixed-effects fits are sensitive to where they start. A common trick is to first fit the
network without random effects, using the sum of squared errors, and start the
mixed-effects fit from those weights.

```{julia}
function train(objective, model, population, ps, st; epochs, lr, refresh = nothing)
    opt_state = Optimisers.setup(Optimisers.Adam(lr), ps)
    losses = Float32[]
    for _ in 1:epochs
        isnothing(refresh) || refresh(st)
        ∇ = gradient(objective, model, population, ps, st)
        opt_state, ps = Optimisers.update(opt_state, ps, ∇)
        push!(losses, objective(model, population, ps, st))
    end
    return ps, losses
end

rng = Random.Xoshiro(1)
model_fixed = DCM(problem, ann; target = 2)    # no error model needed for SSE
ps_fixed, st_fixed = setup(SSE(), rng, model_fixed)
ps_fixed, losses_fixed = train(SSE(), model_fixed, population, ps_fixed, st_fixed; epochs = 150, lr = 0.02f0)
losses_fixed[[1, end]]
```

## Step 2: the mixed-effects model

`VariationalELBO(idxs)` takes the indices of the ODE parameters that get a random effect.
Here all three do: `1` is `kₐ`, `2` is `CL` and `3` is `V`.

```{julia}
objective = VariationalELBO([1, 2, 3])
ps, st = setup(objective, rng, model, population; init_omega = 0.1)
keys(ps), keys(st)
```

The parameters now hold, next to the network weights `theta`:

- `error`: the residual error parameters,
- `omega`: the covariance `Ω` of the random effects (here `0.1` on the diagonal),
- `phi`: the variational posterior of every individual, a mean `μ` and a Cholesky factor `L`.

The state `st` holds the noise `epsilon` used to sample from the posteriors. Resample it
before each gradient step with `update_epsilon!`. We copy the pre-trained network weights
in, and train.

```{julia}
ps = merge(ps, (theta = ps_fixed.theta,))

ps, losses = train(objective, model, population, ps, st; epochs = 200, lr = 0.01f0,
                   refresh = st -> update_epsilon!(rng, st))
losses[[1, 50, 100, 200]]
```

The loss is the negative ELBO, estimated with one Monte Carlo sample per step, hence it
fluctuates.

```{julia}
fig = Figure(size = (500, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Epoch", ylabel = "Negative ELBO")
lines!(ax, losses)
fig
```

## Step 3: update Ω and the error model

The gradient steps above do not update `omega`, which is estimated in a separate *M-step*,
as in classical EM algorithms for mixed-effects models: it is set to the second moment of
the variational posteriors. `m_step` does this, and also re-estimates the residual error
parameters.

```{julia}
ps_before = ps
ps = m_step(objective, rng, model, population, ps, st; epochs = 20, num_samples = 20, verbose = false)
(omega_before = [ps_before.omega[i, i] for i in 1:3], omega_after = [ps.omega[i, i] for i in 1:3])
```

Alternating gradient steps and M-steps a few times is the usual recipe. Here one round
is enough for the demonstration.

## Predictions

By default `predict` uses each individual's own posterior (`individual = true`). With
`individual = false` it uses the typical parameters `ζ(x)` only. The posterior is a
distribution, so for a point prediction we set the noise to zero, which evaluates the
posterior mean.

```{julia}
st_mean = deepcopy(st)
foreach(e -> e .= 0, st_mean.phi.epsilon)

ŷ_individual = predict(model, population, ps, st_mean)
ŷ_typical = predict(model, population, ps, st_mean; individual = false)

rmse(ŷ) = sqrt(mean(reduce(vcat, [(a .- b) .^ 2 for (a, b) in zip(ŷ, get_y(population))])))
(typical = rmse(ŷ_typical), individual = rmse(ŷ_individual))
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
@assert last(losses_fixed) < 0.5 * first(losses_fixed) "fixed effect SSE did not decrease: $(losses_fixed[[1, end]])"
@assert last(losses) < 0.9 * first(losses) "-ELBO did not decrease: $(losses[[1, end]])"
@assert rmse(ŷ_individual) < rmse(ŷ_typical) "individual predictions are not better than typical ones"
@assert rmse(ŷ_individual) < 1.6 "individual RMSE $(rmse(ŷ_individual)) is far above the usual ≈1.25"
```

The individual predictions have a clearly lower error, as they should: they use information from
the individual's own observations. Plotting a few subjects on a fine time grid needs the
parameters of just that subject. `take_batch` slices `ps` and `st` for a set of
individuals:

```{julia}
grid = Float32.(0:2:120)

function curves(i)
    ps_i, st_i = take_batch(ps, st_mean, [i])
    individual = predict(model, population[i:i], ps_i, st_i; saveat = grid)[1]
    typical = predict(model, population[i:i], ps_i, st_i; individual = false, saveat = grid)[1]
    return individual, typical
end

fig = Figure(size = (900, 500))
for (k, i) in enumerate([1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29])
    local ax = Axis(fig[fld(k - 1, 4) + 1, mod1(k, 4)]; title = "ID $(population[i].id)",
              xlabel = k > 4 ? "Time (h)" : "", ylabel = mod1(k, 4) == 1 ? "mg/L" : "")
    individual, typical = curves(i)
    lines!(ax, grid, typical; color = :gray, linestyle = :dash)
    lines!(ax, grid, individual; color = :firebrick)
    scatter!(ax, get_t(population[i]), get_y(population[i]); color = :black, markersize = 6)
end
fig
```

The dashed gray line is the typical prediction for the covariates of that subject, the red line
the individual prediction. The random effects themselves, one row per parameter, one column
per individual, are available from `get_random_effects`:

```{julia}
η = get_random_effects(ps, st_mean)
(mean_η = vec(mean(η; dims = 2)), sd_η = vec(sqrt.(mean(abs2, η; dims = 2))))
```

::: {.callout-note}
This is a short run to show the mechanics. In practice, train for more epochs with a
decaying learning rate, check that the ELBO has flattened, and alternate gradient steps
with `m_step` until `omega` stops moving.
:::
